title: I would speak to the Almighty (Job 13:3)
word: I would speak to the Almighty
hookLine: Job demands a hearing with God
carry: I would speak to the almighty
last: THE BOOK WON'T LET IT FIT.

cards: By chapter thirteen, each of the friends has had a turn to explain, and Job has had it with them. "Ye are forgers of lies," he tells them, "ye are all physicians of no value." Doctors who can't heal.
Then a line that's almost funny, if it weren't so tired: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." If you'd just stay quiet, that would be your wisdom.
It's hard not to hear the seven silent days behind it. Then he turns away from them entirely, because the friends aren't the ones he needs to talk to.

teach.b: "Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God." The friends have been talking about God. Job wants to talk to God.
Not a lecture, not a guess: a hearing, face to face.
It sounds like a courtroom: "Behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified." He has prepared his case, and he'll argue it.

teach.h: THOUGH HE SLAY ME, YET WILL I TRUST.
teach.b: In the middle of the defiance comes a line people quote in very different moods: "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him." Trust and argument in one breath.
Job doesn't stop believing God is there. That's exactly why he won't stop talking: you only demand a hearing from someone you think is listening. It's an old thread in the Tanakh.
Abraham, hearing that Sodom will be destroyed, asks God, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Moses argues for his people after the golden calf.
Jewish tradition has room for prayer that pushes back, that brings a complaint, that says this isn't fair, to God's face. Job isn't asking his friends to let him off. He's asking God to show up.
That's a kind of faith too, the kind that won't go quiet.

how: Jewish tradition includes prayer that questions and argues with God, from Abraham at Sodom and Moses after the golden calf to Job, and these texts are read and studied as part of the Tanakh.

games.q: what does “i would speak to the almighty” mean?
o: Job's plea for his friends to speak on his behalf
Job's wish to argue his case with God himself
Job's promise to stay silent before God at last

games.q: Job wants a hearing — tap the pairs.
p: and it should be your wisdom
shall not the Judge of all the earth

s: Job stops believing God is listening
he wants to argue his case with God, which only makes sense if someone's listening.
Job tells his friends their silence would be wisdom
"O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom."
Job is the only person in the Tanakh who argues with God
Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will do right, and Moses argues for his people.

games.q: you're Job. your friends keep telling you to confess and accept correction. what do you do?
o: apologize for whatever you must have done.
stop speaking to God at all.
turn from your friends and ask for a hearing with God.
games.why: "surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God." he has ordered his cause and wants to argue it face to face.

practice: Is something in your life not fair, not someone else's case, but yours? Say it inside in one or two plain sentences, the way you'd lay out facts to a judge: this happened, this is what it cost, this is what I don't understand.
If you pray, you can say it to God as plainly as Job did; if not, say it to the quiet and hear yourself say it.

wordCard.voice: I would speak to the Almighty. Job turns from his friends and asks for a hearing with God, to argue his case face to face. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Almighty; a name for God, here in Job 13:3.

carryVoice: Your line: I would speak to the almighty. To God, not only about God. Day eight hundred forty-three, done.
